sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye goes first to the three big numbers (3.8%, €64.20, 12.4k), then drops to the orange bar chart, where Saturday's tall bar and Sunday's short one stand out. It reads as a small bakery's admin dashboard for the owner. It feels calm, clean and a little warm. Job (assumed): give the shop owner a quick health check of sales and subscriptions. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

The whole piece:
- One sentence for what it's for: yes
- Main image and headline make one idea: yes ("Shop overview" with KPI cards and a chart, which suits a dashboard)
- Every element does a job: yes
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished: yes
- Repeated elements consistent: yes (the three cards share one structure; unit glyphs are treated the same way in each)
- Colors, shapes and directions carry the mood: yes
- Headings name their sections: yes

No `no` or `unsure` lines, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

There is one point the checklist has no line for (taste, minor): the time frame is unclear. Two cards say "Last 30 days" (left and middle cards, about y 260). The third card says "As of 30 September 2026" and compares with "vs 31 August" (right card, about y 260–284). The chart covers "orders delivered in September 2026" (source line, y 736). A viewer can't tell whether "last 30 days" ends today or on 30 September, so they can't be sure the cards and the chart describe the same period. The fix is one stated reporting period for the whole page, for example a date range beside "Shop overview", or "Last 30 days (1–30 Sep)" on the cards.

**What's working.**
- The page reads as one thing. It uses one accent colour (the bakery orange in the wordmark and the bars), neutral white cards on a pale grey ground, and one sans family, so it looks like this shop's tool and not a patchwork.
- The three KPI cards follow one strict program: label, big figure with a smaller and lighter unit, period, then a green delta. Once you've read one card you can read all three at a glance.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Entries read; I'm settling the two borderline lines and writing the report.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?"** In each KPI card, the label ("Checkout conversion rate", about 16 px regular grey, y≈177) and the line under the number ("Last 30 days" / "As of 30 September 2026", about 14 px regular grey, y≈261) look nearly the same in size, weight and colour. Only the large number between them keeps them apart. So the label, which names what the number means, doesn't read as the card's title. It reads as one more grey caption, and the reader has to work a little harder to tie each number to its name. The chart title "Orders by delivery day" (about 17 px bold, y≈374) does the same job for its panel, but it is set differently from the card labels, so the page has two heading styles for one level.
   - **Why:** Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8: a difference of one step looks like an accident, not a choice. Bringhurst §3.1.1: sizes should come from a small, deliberate scale.
   - **Fix:** make the card label differ obviously from the sub-line, for example by darker colour or medium weight. Better still, set the card labels and the chart title in one shared panel-heading style, and keep 14 px grey for the period and comparison lines.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- The KPI numbers (about 48 px bold, near-black) are far larger and heavier than everything else, so the top row is plainly where to start. The eye reads it left to right like a sentence. Three equal numbers is intended here: on an overview where all three metrics matter, putting one above the others would be wrong.
- The units (%, €, k) are set lighter and smaller than the figures. The numbers lead and the units recede, which gives the cards their strong look without adding another size step.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct, no near-equal sizes)

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One grid holds the whole page.** The logo, the "Shop overview" title, the left KPI card and the chart card all start at the same left edge, about x 48. The three KPI cards (x 48–427, 451–829, 853–1232) use equal gutters of about 24 px. The gap between the card row and the chart card is also about 24 px, and the chart card spans the full width of the three cards above it, ending at the same right edge (x ≈ 1232). Every block lands on the same column lines, so the page reads as one system rather than separate parts placed one by one (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*). Keep this structure if cards are added.
- **The KPI cards line up across their columns.** Each card has the same inner padding (about 26 px), and every row of text sits on a shared baseline in all three cards: label (y ≈ 177), large figure (≈ 222), period line (≈ 260) and change line (≈ 283). Your eye can read across the row and compare like with like, for example the three change figures. Inside each card the lines are spaced tightly, and there is clearly more space between cards, so each card reads as one unit.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The bottom margin under the chart card is about 34 px, against 48 px at the sides. This is probably where the viewport cut off, not the design. Check in a live browser that the page bottom uses the same 48 px margin.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **A clean type scale.** The KPI numbers are big and bold, about 48 px. The units (%, €, k) beside them are set smaller and in lighter grey, at about 30 px. The number leads and the unit stays readable but stays back, which follows Refactoring UI's advice to use weight and colour, not another size. You can count about five sizes, and each has a clear job: page title, chart title, KPI value, labels, and axis and source text.
- **Short, complete lines with a reference point.** Each comparison line says what it is measured against: "+0.4 pts vs previous 30 days", "+6.3% vs 31 August". The "As of 30 September 2026" line makes clear that subscribers are a snapshot while the other two figures cover a period. The source line under the chart names both the system and the period. A stranger has no gap to fill.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The grey axis labels, the source line at the bottom (about y 736) and the grey sub-labels look like they pass 4.5:1 contrast, but they are small, about 11–12 px. Check the actual grey against white to confirm they reach 4.5:1.
- I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was refused. I judged the small text from the full 1280×800 image, which is about one screen and was shown at full size, so close-up detail was not lost.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes).** Image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. A light SaaS dashboard for a bakery's shop owner.
1. Small palette: yes. Gray neutrals, one rust-orange (logo and bars), and green for status.
2. Saturated colour kept to a small share: yes. The orange is only the bars and the logo, roughly a tenth of the area.
3. Clear light-dark range: yes. Dark numerals and labels on white. The cards sit on a very pale gray, but the text values carry the structure.
4. Warm forward, cool back: yes. The warm bars are the only strong colour, set on cool grays.
5. Matching colours look the same: yes. The logo orange is a shade darker than the bars, which reads as a deliberate darkening for text contrast, not a mismatch.
6. No vibrating edges: yes.
7. Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes. Green marks improvements, and all three are rises in good metrics.
8. Meaning not shown by colour alone: yes. The green deltas also have ▲ and a + sign.
9. Dark theme: yes (it's a light theme, so this doesn't apply).

No line answered no or unsure, so there were no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One brand hue does all the work.** The rust-orange appears only in the wordmark and the chart bars. Everything else is gray, white or near-black, so the chart is the only strongly coloured thing on the page and the brand still reads. Keep the orange off the cards, the nav and the headings.
- **Green is kept for one job.** It appears only on the three "vs previous" deltas, and each delta also has an ▲ and a + sign. The good news shows without the page turning into a dashboard full of colours, and it still reads for someone who can't tell red from green. If a metric ever falls, use red together with a ▼, not red alone.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The wordmark is plain set type in one rust-orange. It is recognisable at its small size and would work in one colour. It has generous clear space: about 40 px before the "Overview" nav item and a full empty header band. That keeps the brand mark clean (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*).
- The three green triangles are identical in size, weight and position, so they read as one system of trend marks rather than three separate ornaments.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure. Nine lines are trivially yes because the piece has no photos, illustrations, textures or scenes. Only the logo lines and the icon-consistency line had something to judge.

Walk (Charts and data), working notes:

1. Form fits data: yes (bars compare the seven weekdays)
2. Series can be followed: yes (one series)
3. Ink is data: yes (pale gridlines, flat bars)
4. Honest scales: yes (zero baseline, even ticks of 300 from 0 to 1,200)
5. Enough range or sample: yes (a full month, and the question is the weekday split, not a trend)
6. Palette fits data: yes (one hue for one category series)
7. Readable without colour vision: yes (one series, labelled on the x axis)
8. Few colours: yes
9. Direct labels: yes (no legend needed)
10. Axis values, units, labels: yes (the title says "Orders", the y ticks are counts, and the source line gives the period)
11. Labels clear of marks: yes
12. Title states the finding: **no**. The title "Orders by delivery day" (74,374) names the topic, not the Friday and Saturday peak or the Sunday drop.
13. Bars sorted: yes (natural weekday order)
14. Estimates marked: yes (none shown)
15. Headline numbers have a comparison: yes (all three KPI cards)
16. Key figures on first screen: yes

Bash was refused, so I could not run the crop or entries scripts. I worked from the whole image, which is one screen (1280×800). I did not open the entry for line 12 either. It is marked off-list, so I could not cite it anyway, and I judged the line as taste.

---

**Section.** Charts and data: applies (three KPI cards and one bar chart).

**Findings**
1. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** No. The title "Orders by delivery day" (about x 74, y 374) names the chart's topic. It doesn't say what the chart shows: Saturday is the busiest day at about 1,130 orders, Friday is close behind at about 1,040, and Sunday drops to about 380, roughly a third of Saturday. A bakery owner can read this from the bars quickly. But the title also tells someone skimming the dashboard what to act on, such as staffing and baking capacity at the end of the week, and right now they have to work that out for themselves. Fix: keep the topic as a small label and add a sentence title or caption that says the finding, e.g. "Friday and Saturday carry the week; Sunday is a third of Saturday." Taste: the source for this rule is off the approved list, so this is my judgment. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The bar chart is honest and plain. The y axis starts at zero with even ticks of 300, the gridlines are pale, there is one flat colour and no legend, and the days run in their natural Monday to Sunday order. The Sunday drop and the weekend peak therefore show at true scale with nothing in the way.
- Each KPI card gives its number with a period and a change against the previous period ("+0.4 pts vs previous 30 days", "+€2.10", "+6.3% vs 31 August"). That tells the owner both the level and the direction, and "pts" correctly marks a change in a rate rather than a percentage change.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 15 yes, 1 no (title states the finding)

I've finished the checklist walk and opened the entries. Here is the report.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the four top navigation links, so most lines pass because there's nothing on the screen for them to judge.

**Findings**
1. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** No. There's no date range picker, filter or search anywhere on the screen. The periods are fixed: the KPI cards say "Last 30 days" or "As of 30 September 2026" (y≈260), and the chart says "September 2026" only in the source line (y≈736). A shop owner's most common next question is "how did last week (or last year) compare?" To answer it they have to leave this page, or they simply can't. The period, which frames every number here, is also only stated in small grey text, three times in three different wordings. Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics, #7 (flexibility and efficiency of use). Fix: add one period control next to the "Shop overview" title (around x 1100–1230, y 108) that drives the cards and the chart together, and have it display the active period. That also replaces the scattered period lines. Convention. Weight: minor. The dashboard still does its main job of showing this month's state at a glance.

**What's working.**
- **The current page shows in the nav.** "Overview" (x≈249–319, y≈28) is bold and near-black, while the other three links are regular weight and mid-grey. It matches the "Shop overview" page title, so you know where you are without any extra marker. This is the standard web pattern for a top bar: logo on the left, links in a row. It's also the level of signal a four-item bar needs. Keep it, but don't let it get lighter. Weight plus colour is the minimum here, and an underline would make it sturdier.
- **The nav matches the content.** The nav items Orders, Subscribers and Products line up with what the cards report (order value, active subscribers), so the product's structure is clear from one screen.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicator on the nav links (2 px or more, 3:1 contrast): check by tabbing through in a browser.
- Whether the KPI cards and chart link through to Orders and Subscribers. Nothing on them looks clickable. If they are links, they need a visible sign. If they aren't, that's a missed shortcut on a dashboard.
- Hover states on the grey nav links.
- Target size: the nav links look text-sized, about 16 px glyphs. Their centres are about 75 px apart, though, so they pass WCAG 2.5.8's spacing exception even if the hit areas are only as big as the text.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 1 no (shortcuts for frequent actions), 1 unsure (focus indicator at least 2 px with 3:1); the line on a focused control being hidden by sticky headers is answered yes because nothing on the screen overlaps the nav.
